message: Detected user input used to manually construct a SQL string. This is usually bad practice because manual construction could accidentally result in a SQL injection. An attacker could use a SQL injection to steal or modify contents of the database. Instead, use a parameterized query which is available by default in most database engines. Alternatively, consider using an object-relational mapper (ORM) such as SQLAlchemy which will protect your queries.
confidence_reasoning: The code clearly builds a SQL string using f-string interpolation of column names derived from unsanitized, attacker-controlled JSON keys, which is a real and dangerous pattern (mass assignment combined with dynamic SQL column injection). This aligns well with the semgrep rule's intent even though the VALUES clause itself is parameterized.
supporting_evidence: In the /api/register endpoint, `columns = ["username", "password_hash"] + extra_keys` where extra_keys are arbitrary keys taken directly from the user-supplied JSON body (`data`). These column names are then interpolated directly into the SQL string via an f-string: `f"INSERT INTO users ({','.join(columns)}) VALUES ({placeholders})"`. While the VALUES are parameterized with '?', the column/table identifiers cannot be parameterized in SQLite and are instead concatenated raw from attacker-controlled input. An attacker can submit a JSON body with a malicious key name (e.g. containing a closing paren and additional SQL) to break out of the intended column list and inject arbitrary SQL, since SQLite supports multiple statements via `execute` in some drivers or can still manipulate the query structure. This is a legitimate SQL injection risk via column-name/mass-assignment injection, matching the semgrep tainted-sql-string pattern.
counter_evidence: The VALUES portion of the query is properly parameterized with '?', so the values themselves are not vulnerable to injection. If the underlying sqlite3 driver's execute() only allows a single statement (no stacked queries), the practical exploitability may be limited to schema-level manipulation (e.g., inserting into unintended columns) rather than full arbitrary SQL execution, though this is still a serious injection class (mass assignment / identifier injection).

The surrounding code even has a comment acknowledging 'string-built SQL query instead of parameterized query', confirming the developer intent matches the vulnerable pattern. This directly matches the semgrep rule for tainted SQL string construction from user input.

While the value is parameterized, the column name `key` is not validated against an allow-list and is directly interpolated into the SQL string via an f-string. An attacker can supply an arbitrary key (e.g. `id = 1; DROP TABLE users; --` or subqueries) causing SQL injection, since SQLite/most DB drivers cannot parameterize identifiers. If the application only used known DB column names in practice, exploitation might be limited to existing columns, but no allow-list check exists in the code to prevent malicious key names.

This is a textbook eval injection vulnerability allowing arbitrary Python code execution.
